row.basis: Creation of vegetation
row.note: The commentary’s third “who” names the Lord by bringing forth pasture; Genesis has God command the earth to sprout seed-bearing vegetation, placing plant emergence within the creation scene.

row.basis: Green plants as animal food
row.note: The commentary reads merʿā as pasture seen by the mouths that eat it; Genesis assigns green plants to the beasts, making the pasture’s animal sustenance explicit.

row.basis: Hebrew רעה, tending a flock
row.note: The commentary records Arabic merʿā under r-ʿ-y; Genesis uses the likely cognate Hebrew root רעה for Joseph tending the flock, showing the pastoral action in its own narrative rather than treating the Arabic noun as a dictionary gloss.

row.basis: Pasture and household livelihood
row.note: The commentary places green pasture outside the tent and among the foundations of pastoral life; Jacob’s sons explain that they have come to settle where pasture is available for their flocks, showing its material role in a herding household.

row.basis: Grass for livestock and human fullness
row.note: The commentary says pasture feeds the herd that sustains people; Moses promises grass in the fields for livestock and food until the people are full, joining the two beneficiaries.

row.basis: Rain where no human lives
row.note: The commentary notes that 87:4 names neither rain nor soil and shifts attention to the one who brings out grass; Job describes God sending rain on land without people, supplying the omitted weather source while stressing divine agency beyond human cultivation.

row.basis: Grass brought forth in wilderness
row.note: The commentary treats pasture as something the Lord brings out of hidden ground; Job says the rain makes grass sprout in desolate places, a direct picture of vegetation appearing by divine provision.

row.basis: Hebrew רעה, the Lord as shepherd
row.note: The commentary notes that merʿā belongs to the r-ʿ-y family also used for a shepherd’s work; Psalm 23 predicates that Hebrew cognate of the Lord, making explicit the pastoral sense that the Qur’anic wording leaves implicit.

row.basis: Green pasture and rest
row.note: The commentary says merʿā unites grass, grazing place, and the act of grazing; the psalm’s shepherd makes the speaker lie down in green pastures and leads him beside water, bringing those linked images together.

row.basis: Watering furrows and blessing growth
row.note: The commentary reads pasture as the land’s recurring yield under the Lord’s measure; the psalm describes God watering furrows and softening earth so its growth is blessed, joining measured water to yield.

row.basis: Pastures, flocks, and grain at year’s end
row.note: The commentary calls pasture the land’s annual yield for herds; the psalm pictures pastures clothed with flocks and valleys covered with grain, then making joyful sounds, a close pastoral harvest scene.

row.basis: Grass for cattle, plants for people
row.note: The commentary says the word merʿā views vegetation as food for the creature that grazes; the psalm says God makes grass grow for cattle and plants for human work, naming the same giver and both uses.

row.basis: Every creature waits for food in season
row.note: The commentary treats pasture as one creature’s provision from the Lord; the psalm says all creatures wait for God to give food at its proper time, expanding the individual pasture into universal dependence.

row.basis: Renewing the face of the ground
row.note: The commentary follows green growth into decay and sees the Lord as the source of emergence; the psalm says God sends forth spirit and renews the ground, giving the vegetation cycle a creation-and-renewal frame.

row.basis: Praise in response to creation
row.note: The commentary begins with a command to glorify the Lord and identifies him through creation and pasture; the psalmist vows to sing to the Lord while alive, placing praise directly in response to the created order.

row.basis: Clouds, rain, and grass on hills
row.note: The commentary hears the unmentioned rain behind the pasture that God brings forth; the psalm explicitly connects God’s cloud-cover and rain with grass growing on the mountains.

row.basis: Food for beasts from the same giver
row.note: The commentary says pasture names vegetation as the herd’s food; the psalm says God gives food to animals and young ravens, extending the provision claim beyond the flock.

row.basis: Teaching descending like rain and dew
row.note: The commentary links the grass passage to the later recitation and instruction; Moses asks that his teaching fall like rain and his speech distill like dew, joining divine teaching to the water that makes growth possible.

row.basis: Rain yields seed and bread
row.note: The commentary reads pasture as growth produced by water and later contrasts it with the recited word; Isaiah says rain and snow water earth, making it yield seed for sowing and bread for eating, a precise provision chain.

row.basis: The spoken word accomplishes its purpose
row.note: The commentary connects the Lord who brings out pasture with the word later recited and retained; Isaiah’s next verse says the word from God’s mouth does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose, explicitly setting word beside the rain-and-seed image.

row.basis: Grass fades while God’s word stands
row.note: The commentary contrasts the pasture that becomes dark debris with the recitation that remains; Isaiah says grass withers but God’s word stands forever, giving the same concrete contrast between perishable vegetation and enduring speech.

row.basis: The earth gives birth to the dead
row.note: The commentary treats recurring growth from dead ground as a sign that the dead can be brought out; Isaiah calls the earth to give birth to its dead, making the earth’s production image explicitly serve resurrection hope.

row.basis: A heavenly command over each blade of grass
row.note: The commentary presents each emergence of pasture as a gift whose hidden growth belongs to God; this midrash says no blade of grass lacks a heavenly constellation that strikes it and commands it to grow, interpreting ordinary growth as supervised providence.

row.basis: Seed grows while the sower does not know how
row.note: The commentary describes growth from an unseen seed and root as an act whose source is the Lord; Jesus’ parable says the seed sprouts and grows while the person who scattered it does not know how, making hidden growth the point of the image.

row.basis: Earth yields successive stages
row.note: The commentary follows pasture from concealed seed to visible green; the parable says the earth produces first a blade, then an ear, then full grain, a direct sequence of emergence and maturation.

row.basis: Growth reaches harvest
row.note: The commentary calls pasture the land’s yield and follows it to its later end; Jesus’ parable ends when the grain is ripe and the sickle is put in, tying emergence to the harvest that follows.

row.basis: God gives the growth
row.note: The commentary insists that the Lord, rather than the human observer, is the one who brings pasture out; Paul says neither planter nor waterer counts, but God who gives the growth, an explicit account of divine agency in cultivation.

row.basis: A seed dies before it comes to life
row.note: The commentary reads pasture’s greening and subsequent decay as an analogy that makes resurrection imaginable; Paul says what is sown does not come to life unless it dies, using the plant cycle as his argument for resurrection.

row.basis: Perishable sowing and imperishable raising
row.note: The commentary contrasts grass that ends as debris with the human future that is raised into what lasts; Paul explicitly contrasts what is sown perishable with what is raised imperishable.

row.basis: All flesh is like grass
row.note: The commentary follows pasture from green growth to its end; Peter quotes Isaiah that all flesh is grass and its glory like a flower, applying vegetation’s short life to human life.

row.basis: The Lord’s word endures as gospel proclamation
row.note: The commentary contrasts the grass that withers with the recitation that remains; Peter says the Lord’s word endures and identifies it with the good news preached to the readers, making the word/grass contrast an apostolic proclamation claim.

row.basis: Creation grounds praise
row.note: The commentary’s praise call is followed by claims about the Lord creating and sustaining pasture; Revelation’s elders praise the Lord as worthy because he created all things, a compact Christian doxology grounded in creation.

row.basis: Created food calls for thanksgiving
row.note: The commentary joins the Lord’s creative provision of pasture to glorification; the Didache’s meal thanksgiving says the Almighty created all things and gave food and drink so people might thank him, making the provision-to-praise relation liturgical.

row.basis: Field growth before rain or cultivation
row.note: The commentary emphasizes that 87:4 leaves soil and rain unnamed and foregrounds the one who brings pasture out; Genesis describes the field before rain and before a human works the ground, clarifying the conditions whose absence the short Qur’anic clause leaves unstated.

row.basis: God makes trees grow from the ground
row.note: The commentary describes grass rising from hidden seed and soil; Genesis says God makes trees grow from the ground, a related but broader account of vegetation’s emergence.

row.basis: Moses leads a flock to Horeb
row.note: The commentary recalls Moses’ years as a shepherd and links that work to his later encounter at the fire; Exodus places Moses at Horeb while leading his father-in-law’s flock, grounding the shepherd-to-revelation sequence in another scripture.

row.basis: Theophany while Moses is tending sheep
row.note: The commentary moves from Moses’ staff for tending sheep to the fire where revelation begins; Exodus has the bush blaze before Moses in the same scene, preserving the concrete meeting of pastoral work and divine appearance.

row.basis: Abraham trusts God to provide
row.note: The commentary presents Abraham’s Lord as the one who feeds and sustains him; at the binding of Isaac, Abraham tells his son that God will provide the offering, giving divine provision a specific Abrahamic scene.

row.basis: Abraham receives Isaac back from death
row.note: The commentary’s Abrahamic sequence names the Lord as the one who kills and gives life; Hebrews says Abraham reasoned that God could raise Isaac and so received him back figuratively from death, interpreting the binding story through resurrection.

row.basis: Blessing after eating one is full
row.note: The commentary presents grass and food as a free gift that ends in glorifying the giver; Moses commands Israel to bless the Lord after eating and becoming full, making gratitude the human response to provision.

row.basis: Harvest left for the poor and sojourner
row.note: The commentary says a yield received without payment still carries a duty to give others their share; Leviticus forbids harvesting a field to its edge and leaves gleanings for the poor and the sojourner, specifying the social obligation attached to produce.

row.basis: A forgotten sheaf belongs to the vulnerable
row.note: The commentary connects free yield with giving a due from the harvest; Deuteronomy leaves a forgotten sheaf for the sojourner, orphan, and widow, turning that connection into a concrete harvest law.

row.basis: A cut tree can sprout again
row.note: The commentary takes recurring green growth as evidence that life can emerge after apparent death; Job says a felled tree can sprout again when it smells water, then contrasts that hope with human mortality, making the plant-to-human analogy vivid but unsettled.

row.basis: Job leaves human resurrection as a question
row.note: The commentary uses grass renewed from the earth to make the dead’s return plausible; after describing a tree’s regrowth, Job asks whether a dead human can live again, so the same natural analogy ends in an open question rather than an asserted answer.

row.basis: A fruitful tree beside water
row.note: The commentary says growth follows from water and that the visible green is a gift; the righteous person in the psalm is like a tree planted by streams that yields fruit in season, giving water-fed vegetation an ethical image.

row.basis: Chaff blown away
row.note: The commentary’s pasture becomes dark debris and illustrates the passing life of this world; the psalm calls the wicked chaff driven by wind, using light plant remains for a moral image rather than a botanical cycle.

row.basis: Grass that flourishes and withers in a day
row.note: The commentary follows the pasture’s green life into decay; the psalm compares human life to grass that flourishes in the morning and withers by evening, applying the same daily plant arc to mortality.

row.basis: Human days like grass
row.note: The commentary sets pasture’s brief green phase against what lasts beyond this life; the psalm says a human’s days are like grass and flourish like a field flower, making the plant’s brevity a figure for human transience.

row.basis: Wind erases the flower’s place
row.note: The commentary says the plant is turned into debris and disappears; the psalm says wind passes over the field flower and it is gone so its place knows it no more, sharpening the disappearance image.

row.basis: Mercy outlasts human life
row.note: The commentary turns from pasture’s short life to the Hereafter as better and more enduring; the psalm contrasts grass-like human days with the Lord’s everlasting steadfast love, supplying a close theological contrast of mortal vegetation and lasting divine good.

row.basis: Attend carefully to the flock
row.note: The commentary gives the shepherd’s work a sense of watching over the herd and its future; Proverbs tells the keeper to know the state of his flock and attend to the herds, making that practical oversight explicit in its own pastoral setting.

row.basis: The divine shepherd settles the flock in good pasture
row.note: The commentary says the Qur’anic clause names the one who brings pasture but does not call God a shepherd; Ezekiel explicitly depicts God feeding his flock and settling it in good pasture, showing how another scripture makes the shepherd-pasture connection explicit.

row.basis: God’s word runs through the earth
row.note: The commentary juxtaposes the Lord’s pasture-making with the Prophet’s recitation; elsewhere in the same psalm God sends his command through the earth before the cloud, grass, and animal-food lines, placing word and created provision within one hymn.

row.basis: A green tree endures drought by water
row.note: The commentary’s plant grows and then withers, while its creator sustains life; Jeremiah pictures a tree planted by water whose leaf stays green and which does not cease bearing fruit in drought, a counter-image of sustained rather than seasonal growth.

row.basis: Blessing acknowledges the world’s owner
row.note: The commentary says the Lord provides pasture without demanding a fee; the rabbis teach that one may not enjoy the world before blessing God, because the earth belongs to God, adding human acknowledgment to apparently free provision.

row.basis: A blessing for produce of the ground
row.note: The commentary begins with glorification and then names vegetation as the Lord’s provision; the Mishnah assigns a blessing to fruit of the ground, showing how ordinary produce becomes a spoken act of praise.

row.basis: Field grass is temporary yet clothed by God
row.note: The commentary describes pasture becoming dark debris and treats vegetation as provision from its maker; Jesus says grass is in the field today and thrown into the oven tomorrow, yet God clothes it, joining transience to divine care.

row.basis: Pasture through the gate
row.note: The commentary notes that merʿā carries pasture and grazing while the root also names a shepherd’s work; Jesus says those entering through him will be saved and find pasture, placing the pasture image in a Christian shepherd-and-access teaching.

row.basis: Human planting and watering depend on God
row.note: The commentary emphasizes that the Lord, not the human observer, brings pasture out; Paul describes himself planting and Apollos watering before saying God caused growth, distinguishing human labor from the source of life.

row.basis: The rich person fades like a field flower
row.note: The commentary uses the plant’s short life to frame the contrast between this world and what endures; James says the rich person passes away like grass and its flower, applying the same fading image to worldly status.

row.basis: Recurring seasons and harvest
row.note: The commentary treats pasture as the land’s recurring annual yield; Genesis promises that seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter will continue while the earth remains, giving that cycle a covenant frame.

row.basis: Rain before field produce
row.note: The commentary notes that the pasture clause itself omits rain; the immediately preceding verse promises rain in its seasons so Israel can gather grain, wine, and oil, supplying the source and agricultural continuation beside the grass-for-livestock verse.

row.basis: Hebrew מַרְעִיתוֹ, flock of his pasture
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic merʿā with root r-ʿ-y and says it can name pasture as well as grazing; this psalm uses a cognate Hebrew pasture noun for God’s flock, joining the grazing ground to the creatures that depend on it.

row.basis: Wilderness changed to pools and springs
row.note: The commentary describes pasture appearing in dry, uneven ground as a distinct gift; the psalm says God turns wilderness into pools and parched land into springs, a direct reversal from barrenness to life-sustaining water.

row.basis: Fields sown for fruitful yield
row.note: The commentary calls pasture the earth’s yield and connects it to the survival of households; the psalm’s hungry settlers sow fields and plant vineyards that produce fruit, extending divine restoration into human cultivation and livelihood.

row.basis: God dries the green tree and makes the dry flourish
row.note: The commentary follows pasture from green growth into dark debris; Ezekiel puts both reversals under God’s hand, who can dry a green tree and make a dry tree flourish, making divine control of both sides of the cycle explicit.

row.basis: Water on dry land and spirit on descendants
row.note: The commentary reads pasture as new life brought out of hidden ground and points to resurrection; Isaiah promises water on thirsty land and God’s spirit on descendants, joining soil’s renewal to the renewal of a people.

row.basis: Descendants sprout among grass by streams
row.note: The commentary connects pasture’s emergence with a later spiritual and human emergence; Isaiah pictures descendants sprouting among grass like willows beside flowing water, giving the same water-fed growth an explicit communal meaning.

row.basis: Righteousness and praise spring up like a garden
row.note: The commentary makes the Lord’s pasture-making the ground for praise and connects plant emergence with moral instruction; Isaiah says God makes righteousness and praise spring up before the nations like earth’s growth and a garden’s seed, joining vegetation to public praise.

row.basis: Wilderness pastures turn green again
row.note: The commentary presents the green pasture as a gift that may later wither; Joel addresses the animals and says the wilderness pastures become green and the trees bear fruit after devastation, making restored pasture a concrete sign of recovery.

row.basis: Sowing righteousness until rain comes
row.note: The commentary develops pasture’s yield into a lesson about what sustains life and what endures; Hosea commands the people to sow righteousness, reap steadfast love, break fallow ground, and seek God until he rains righteousness upon them, turning cultivation into an ethical summons.

row.basis: A tithe of the land’s yield belongs to God
row.note: The commentary says the pasture arrives without a fee yet connects produce with a due given at harvest; Leviticus declares the tithe of seed and tree fruit holy to the Lord, adding a distinct claim of divine ownership over the yield.

row.basis: God’s word sustains beyond crop production
row.note: The commentary places the Lord’s pasture provision beside the recited word; Wisdom says the manna teaches that crops themselves do not sustain people apart from God’s word, a precise Jewish reflection on food and divine speech.

row.basis: Blessing on seeing blossoming trees
row.note: The commentary moves from visible new growth to glorifying its giver; the Talmud prescribes a blessing when one sees trees budding in Nisan, thanking God for a world that lacks nothing and for good trees made for human enjoyment.

row.basis: Field flowers grow without human toil
row.note: The commentary says that grass emerges by the Lord’s action and is received without payment; Jesus points to lilies growing without labor or spinning as evidence of God’s care, making unworked growth a concrete sign of provision.

row.basis: Rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness
row.note: The commentary identifies the Lord through pasture and says its yield is freely given; Paul tells his hearers that God gives rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling people with food and gladness, a compact Christian witness to the same provision chain.

row.basis: Seed, bread, and a harvest of righteousness
row.note: The commentary connects annual yield with a duty to give from what the land produces; Paul says God supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, then multiplies seed and the harvest of righteousness, joining provision to generosity.

row.basis: Called out of darkness into light
row.note: The commentary reads vegetation’s emergence from hidden soil as an image for people brought from ignorance into light through scripture; Peter describes God calling a people out of darkness into marvelous light, giving that extraction image a communal and instructional form.

row.basis: Light shines from darkness into hearts
row.note: The commentary compares a shoot emerging from dark soil with people brought from darkness to light by teaching; Paul invokes the Creator’s command that light shine from darkness and applies it to knowledge shining in human hearts, connecting creation speech with inward illumination.

row.basis: Grain dies and bears much fruit
row.note: The commentary treats the pasture’s passage from life to decay as a sign that death need not be the final state; Jesus says a grain falling into the earth must die to bear much fruit, using the plant’s death as a distinct Christian account of life emerging through death.

row.basis: Seed decays and rises to bear fruit
row.note: The commentary uses the pasture’s emergence and later decay to make resurrection imaginable; Clement describes dry seed falling into the earth and decaying before the Lord’s providence raises it into many fruitful plants, an explicit early Christian reading of vegetation as resurrection evidence.

row.basis: Uneven yields from different ground
row.note: The commentary pictures green pasture appearing patchily, with bare earth beside it; in Jesus’ sower parable the seed falls on good soil and yields at different rates, a specific agricultural image of uneven ground and growth.

row.basis: The flock’s milk supports its keeper
row.note: The commentary traces pasture from grass to the herd and then to human livelihood through milk, wool, and work; Paul asks whether a shepherd tends a flock without sharing its milk, making the animal-to-human support chain explicit in an argument about labor.

row.basis: The farmer waits for fruit and seasonal rains
row.note: The commentary links the plant’s temporary cycle with the later judgment and what endures; James tells believers to wait like a farmer for the earth’s precious fruit until the early and late rains, turning the crop cycle into a picture of eschatological patience.

row.basis: The earth’s ripe harvest at judgment
row.note: The commentary places pasture’s short-lived growth before the surah’s final warnings; Revelation depicts the earth’s harvest as ripe and ready for reaping, giving agricultural growth an explicit end-time judgment image.

row.basis: Different measures of fruit from good soil
row.note: The commentary stresses that vegetation appears in patches rather than as a uniform carpet; Jesus interprets the good soil as yielding thirty, sixty, or a hundredfold, making variation in the fruit of receptive ground explicit.

row.basis: Human life like field grass
row.note: The commentary follows pasture’s brief green phase into decay and relates that passing life to the Hereafter; Isaiah calls all flesh grass and its glory a field flower, explicitly extending the vegetation image to human transience.

row.basis: New birth from imperishable seed through the word
row.note: The commentary links plant emergence to human learning and then contrasts fading grass with retained recitation; Peter says believers are born again from imperishable seed through the living word, directly joining agricultural generation to enduring proclamation.

row.basis: Hidden things brought to light
row.note: The commentary says pasture comes from an unseen place and connects emergence with God’s knowledge of what is hidden; Paul says the Lord will bring hidden things to light and disclose the heart’s purposes, giving that hidden-to-manifest relation an ethical and eschatological use.
